MA plot, volcano plot, and p-value histogram saved.

steps.name: Effect-size tiering and lfcThreshold testing
caveats: A fold-change threshold is a convention, not a biological constant; the report must say so rather than implying 0.5 or 1.0 marks a mechanistic boundary.
'Large but not significant' genes are usually low-count or high-variance and should be presented as hypothesis-generating only.
Cohen's d on VST values assumes approximate normality per group; with n=60 per group this is tolerable but should be stated.
Group-mean fold change can be driven by a subset of samples — the heatmap is there to expose that, and any tier-1 gene whose signal comes from a handful of samples must be called out.
steps.context: This is the step the research question's second clause asks for. The key methodological point is that filtering a theta=0 result by fold change is a common but statistically loose practice; DESeq2's lfcThreshold test is the principled version and both should be reported so the difference is visible.
steps.question: Of the genes that differ between cases and controls, which differences are large enough to matter — and how many significant genes carry fold changes too small to be biologically meaningful?
constraints: State the chosen theta values (0.5 primary, 1.0 secondary) and justify them as conventions, not as data-derived truths; do not silently pick a threshold that maximises the gene count.
Use the apeglm-shrunken LFC for all effect-size ranking and tiering; note where raw and shrunken LFC give materially different tier assignments.
Report the lfcThreshold-test count AND the naive padj+|LFC| intersection count side by side, with the difference explained.
Compute Cohen's d on the VST matrix from T1S1, not on raw counts.
Every tier count must be an absolute number of genes, not only a percentage.
steps.description: Take the full DESeq2 results from T1S2 and separate statistical significance from effect magnitude explicitly. (1) Report the distribution of shrunken |log2FoldChange| among genes with padj < 0.05 — median, quartiles, and the fraction below |LFC| of 0.5 and 1.0 — to quantify directly how much of the significant list is small-effect. Report how many genes pass at each theta and how that number compares to naively intersecting padj<0.05 with |LFC|>theta. Reported counts from the lfcThreshold Wald test at theta=0.5 and theta=1.0, alongside the naive post-hoc intersection counts.
Per-gene Cohen's d with confidence intervals for the top tier, and a note on where LFC-ranking and d-ranking disagree.
Volcano plot with both boundaries drawn and a VST heatmap of the top tier across all 120 samples.

steps.name: Ranked GSEA on the case vs control signature
caveats: GO BP sets are nested and highly overlapping, so significant sets arrive in correlated blocks — collapse or cluster them before reporting a count.

If the gene set collections are unavailable at run time, this step degrades to a reported gap — the DE and effect-size results from T1S2/T1S3 remain the primary answer.
steps.context: Rank-based GSEA is used deliberately instead of over-representation of a thresholded list, because the research question treats the threshold itself as the open issue. GSEA uses the whole ranking and so does not inherit the arbitrariness of the cutoff.
steps.question: Which biological processes are coordinately shifted between the 60 cases and the 60 controls in whole blood, independent of any fold-change cutoff?
constraints: Use ranked GSEA over the full gene list; do not run over-representation analysis on a padj-filtered list as the primary result.

Confirm the human hallmark and GO-BP gene-set resources are present before use; if either is absent, report that plainly and proceed with whatever is available rather than substituting a different organism's sets.
Never use mouse or rat gene sets — the data is Homo sapiens.
Report the identifier mapping rate if any mapping was required.
Explicitly flag pathways whose leading edge consists only of small-effect genes from T1S3.
steps.description: Using the complete ranked gene list from T1S2 (rank by the Wald statistic, or by shrunken log2FoldChange as a sensitivity check — report both and note disagreement), run fgsea against human gene-set collections: the hallmark collection as the primary readout and GO Biological Process as the mechanism-level follow-up. If T1S1 reported that the counts carry Ensembl or Entrez identifiers rather than HGNC symbols, map them to symbols using the staged human UniProt ID-mapping resource first and report the mapping rate and how many genes were lost. Enrichment plots for the top sets in each direction.
A cross-reference showing, for each top pathway, how many of its leading-edge genes fall in the T1S3 'significant and large' tier.
An explicit written assessment of whether the enrichment is consistent with a blood cell-composition shift rather than regulation.

plan.title: Whole-blood case vs control DE with effect-size filtering
plan.analytical_narrative:
The input is a single-batch human whole-blood bulk RNA-seq experiment: gene-level Salmon counts for 12,000 genes across 121 columns (one is the gene identifier column, 120 samples) plus a 120-row metadata table carrying one condition column with 60 cases and 60 controls. The question has two halves — which genes differ (a testing problem) and which differences are large enough to matter (an effect-size problem) — so the plan keeps them separate rather than collapsing both into one thresholded gene list.

T1S1 loads the counts, verifies the sample-identifier join against metadata.csv, drops the non-count identifier column, checks that the matrix is integer-valued raw counts (the profile explicitly flags that the record does not state whether a length correction was applied — if values are non-integer TPM/length-scaled, that must be caught before DESeq2 sees them and either rounded with the caveat recorded or handled via a length-aware path), filters low-count genes, and runs a library-size/PCA-based QC that also checks whether the case/control split separates on PC1-PC2 or whether some unlabelled structure (sex, cell-composition, depth) dominates. With 60 vs 60 and a single batch there is no batch term to fit; the sample size is large enough that a hidden compositional axis in whole blood is the main confounding risk, so it is quantified rather than assumed away.

T1S2 runs the actual contrast, cases vs controls, with DESeq2's negative-binomial Wald test on the unpaired two-group design, BH-adjusted. This is where 'which genes differ' is answered. Because 60 vs 60 is well powered, statistical significance alone will flag many genes with trivial fold changes — that is precisely the failure mode the question anticipates. So T1S2 also produces shrunken log2 fold changes (apeglm) so effect sizes are not inflated by low-count noise, and reports the significance-only list alongside its size.

T1S3 answers the second half explicitly. It separates the two axes with a rank-by-effect-size table, an lfcThreshold-based formal test (DESeq2 can test H0:|LFC| <= theta rather than H0:LFC=0, which is the statistically correct way to ask 'is the effect bigger than theta', not a post-hoc filter), and a standardised effect measure per gene so that fold change is interpretable relative to between-sample variability. The output is a tiered gene list: significant-only, significant-and-large, and large-but-not-significant, with an explicit statement of how the tiering thresholds were chosen and of the fact that a fold-change cutoff applied after testing does not control error rate the way the lfcThreshold test does.

T1S4 gives the DE result biological reading via ranked GSEA over the staged human hallmark and GO-BP collections (HGNC symbols; the counts must first be confirmed to carry symbols, and mapped via the staged human UniProt ID-mapping file if they carry Ensembl/Entrez IDs instead). GSEA on the full ranked statistic is used rather than over-representation of a thresholded list, because the whole point of the question is that the threshold is contested — a rank-based test does not depend on it. This step enriches the interpretation; if the gene-set resources turn out to be unavailable at run time it should report that and the DE result still stands.

steps.context: Rank-based GSEA is used deliberately instead of over-representation of a thresholded list, because the research question treats the threshold itself as the open issue. GSEA uses the whole ranking and so does not inherit the arbitrariness of the cutoff.
constraints: Use ranked GSEA over the full gene list; do not run over-representation analysis on a padj-filtered list as the primary result.

Confirm the human hallmark and GO-BP gene-set resources are present before use; if either is absent, report that plainly and proceed with whatever is available rather than substituting a different organism's sets.
Never use mouse or rat gene sets — the data is Homo sapiens.
Report the identifier mapping rate if any mapping was required.
Explicitly flag pathways whose leading edge consists only of small-effect genes from T1S3.
acceptance_criteria: A ranked GSEA results table for hallmark and GO-BP with NES, p-value, BH-adjusted p-value, set size, and leading-edge genes.
Enrichment plots for the top sets in each direction.
A cross-reference showing, for each top pathway, how many of its leading-edge genes fall in the T1S3 'significant and large' tier.
An explicit written assessment of whether the enrichment is consistent with a blood cell-composition shift rather than regulation.
caveats: GO BP sets are nested and highly overlapping, so significant sets arrive in correlated blocks — collapse or cluster them before reporting a count.
Whole-blood signatures are strongly driven by cell-type proportion differences; enrichment alone cannot distinguish composition from regulation, and this must be stated rather than implied away.
If the gene set collections are unavailable at run time, this step degrades to a reported gap — the DE and effect-size results from T1S2/T1S3 remain the primary answer.
